questions.enonce_markdown:
Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F and Ne are the elements of the Period 2 of the Periodic Table.

(i) Sketch a graph of melting points against atomic number for the elements.

(ii) Explain the shape of the graph. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sketch.** Atomic number on the horizontal axis (3 to 10), melting point on the vertical axis. Approximate melting points:

| Element | Li | Be | B | C | N | O | F | Ne |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Atomic number | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
| Structure | metallic | metallic | giant covalent | giant covalent | $\mathrm{N_2}$ molecules | $\mathrm{O_2}$ molecules | $\mathrm{F_2}$ molecules | Ne atoms |
| Melting point / $^\circ$C (approx.) | 181 | 1287 | 2076 | 3550 (sublimes) | $-210$ | $-219$ | $-220$ | $-249$ |

The curve **rises steadily from lithium (low, about 181 $^\circ$C) through beryllium and boron to a maximum at carbon** (the highest point of the graph), then **drops sharply to nitrogen** and stays very low for oxygen, fluorine and neon, which lie almost on the horizontal axis (neon the lowest).

**(ii) Explanation.**

- **Li and Be (metals):** metallic bonding, the attraction between a lattice of positive ions and delocalised electrons. From Li to Be the ions have a higher charge ($\mathrm{Li^+}$, $\mathrm{Be^{2+}}$), are smaller and there are more delocalised electrons per atom, so the metallic bond is stronger and the melting point is higher.
- **B and C:** giant covalent (macromolecular) structures in which every atom is held by strong covalent bonds in a continuous network. A great amount of energy is needed to break these bonds, so the melting points are very high, with the maximum at carbon (diamond or graphite, strong C-C bonds throughout the structure).
- **N, O, F and Ne:** simple molecular substances ($\mathrm{N_2}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$, $\mathrm{F_2}$) or single atoms (Ne). Only weak intermolecular forces (London dispersion forces) act between the particles and are overcome on melting; the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken. The melting points are therefore very low. Neon, a small monatomic gas with only 10 electrons and the weakest dispersion forces, has the lowest melting point.

questions.enonce_markdown:
From the elements of the period lithium to neon, write the formula of:

(i) An oxide which is amphoteric

(ii) A hydride which is a liquid *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** Beryllium oxide, $\mathrm{BeO}$. It is amphoteric: it reacts with acids to form a salt, $\mathrm{BeO} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \rightarrow \mathrm{BeSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}$, and with strong alkalis to form a beryllate, $\mathrm{BeO} + 2\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na_2[Be(OH)_4]}$.

**(ii)** Water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (the hydride of oxygen). It is a liquid at room temperature because of extensive hydrogen bonding between its molecules. The other hydrides of the period ($\mathrm{LiH}$ and $\mathrm{BeH_2}$ are solids; $\mathrm{B_2H_6}$, $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{HF}$, boiling point $19.5^\circ\mathrm{C}$, are gases at room temperature) are not liquids.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The elements of Group IV (Group 14) of the Periodic Table are carbon, silicon, germanium, tin and lead.

(i) Classify the elements as metals, metalloids and non-metals.

| Element | Classification |
|---|---|
| C | |
| Si | |
| Ge | |
| Sn | |
| Pb | |

(ii) Give a chemical equation for the reaction of germanium tetrachloride with water.

(iii) Explain why carbon tetrachloride will NOT react similarly with water as germanium tetrachloride. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

| Element | Classification |
|---|---|
| C | non-metal |
| Si | metalloid (semi-metal) |
| Ge | metalloid (semi-metal) |
| Sn | metal |
| Pb | metal |

**(ii)** Germanium tetrachloride is hydrolysed by water (it fumes in moist air) to hydrated germanium(IV) oxide and hydrogen chloride:

$$\mathrm{GeCl_4(l)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{GeO_2(s)} + 4\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$$

(equivalently $\mathrm{GeCl_4} + 4\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ge(OH)_4} + 4\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{Ge(OH)_4}$ being $\mathrm{GeO_2\cdot 2H_2O}$). Atoms: Ge 1 = 1; Cl 4 = 4; H 4 = 4; O 2 = 2.

**(iii)** Hydrolysis of a tetrachloride requires the central atom to accept a lone pair of electrons from a water molecule, forming an intermediate with more than 8 electrons around the central atom.

- **Germanium** (period 4) has **vacant, low-energy 4d orbitals** in its valence shell, so it can accept a lone pair from the oxygen of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and expand its octet (five- or six-co-ordinate intermediate); then HCl is lost, and hydrolysis takes place.
- **Carbon** (period 2) has **no d orbitals** in its second shell (the maximum is 8 electrons, 2s and 2p only), so it cannot accept a lone pair to form such an intermediate. In addition the small carbon atom is shielded by four large chlorine atoms, which hinders the approach of water. Hence $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ does **not react** with water (it is immiscible with it).

questions.enonce_markdown:
Some of the Group IV elements show "inert pair effect"

(i) What is the "inert pair effect"

(ii) Why is PbO more stable than $\mathrm{PbO_2}$? *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)** The **inert pair effect** is the reluctance of the two outer $s$ electrons ($ns^2$) of the heavier elements of a group (Sn, Pb in Group IV) to take part in bonding. As a result the oxidation state **two lower than the group oxidation state** (+2 instead of +4) becomes more stable down the group. It arises because the $s$ electrons are held tightly (poor shielding by the intervening $d$ and $f$ electrons gives a high effective nuclear charge), so the energy needed to use them in bonding is not recovered by bond formation.

**(ii)** In PbO, lead is in the **+2** oxidation state: only the two $6p$ electrons are used, and the inert $6s^2$ pair stays on the atom. In $\mathrm{PbO_2}$, lead is in the +4 state, which needs the $6s^2$ pair to be involved in bonding. Because of the inert pair effect Pb(IV) is unstable and strongly oxidising (for example $\mathrm{PbO_2}$ oxidises concentrated HCl to chlorine) and tends to be reduced to Pb(II); **PbO is therefore the more stable oxide**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
This question is on the Group VII elements (Halogens).

(i) Complete the following table:

| | Colour at room temperature | Physical state |
|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | | |
| Iodine | | |

(ii) All the halogens show variable oxidation states except fluorine. Explain.

(iii) The following equation is used in iodometric titration

$$\mathrm{IO_3^-(aq)} + \mathrm{I^-(aq)} + \mathrm{H^+(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{I_2(aq)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$$

A: From the reacting species identify the oxidant and reductant.

Oxidant:

Reductant:

B: Give the balanced equation

(iv) Using suitable chemical reagents and stating your observations, clearly explain how you would distinguish between aqueous solutions of potassium chloride and potassium bromide? *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i)**

| | Colour at room temperature | Physical state |
|---|---|---|
| Chlorine | greenish-yellow (pale yellow-green) | gas |
| Iodine | grey-black (shiny dark solid; it gives a violet vapour on warming) | solid |

**(ii)** Fluorine is the most electronegative element and, being in period 2, has **no d orbitals** available in its outer shell (the second shell holds at most 8 electrons), so it cannot promote electrons and expand its octet: it shows only the oxidation states 0 and $-1$ in its compounds. Chlorine, bromine and iodine have **vacant d orbitals** in their outer shell, so paired outer electrons can be promoted to them and unpaired electrons are available for bonding with more electronegative atoms such as oxygen or fluorine; they show variable oxidation states $-1$, $+1$, $+3$, $+5$ and $+7$ (for example $\mathrm{HClO}$, $\mathrm{HClO_2}$, $\mathrm{ClO_3^-}$, $\mathrm{ClO_4^-}$).

**(iii) A.** In $\mathrm{IO_3^-}$ iodine is $+5$ and in $\mathrm{I^-}$ it is $-1$; both form $\mathrm{I_2}$ (oxidation state 0).

- **Oxidant:** $\mathrm{IO_3^-}$ (iodate(V) ion): the oxidation state of iodine falls from $+5$ to $0$ (it is reduced; it accepts electrons).
- **Reductant:** $\mathrm{I^-}$ (iodide ion): the oxidation state of iodine rises from $-1$ to $0$ (it is oxidised; it gives electrons).

**B. Balanced equation.** Half equations: $2\mathrm{IO_3^-} + 12\mathrm{H^+} + 10e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $2\mathrm{I^-} \rightarrow \mathrm{I_2} + 2e^-$ (multiplied by 5). Adding, and dividing by 2:

$$\mathrm{IO_3^-(aq)} + 5\mathrm{I^-(aq)} + 6\mathrm{H^+(aq)} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{I_2(aq)} + 3\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$$

Check: I $1 + 5 = 6 = 3\times2$; O $3 = 3$; H $6 = 6$; charge $-1 - 5 + 6 = 0$.

**(iv) Distinguishing KCl(aq) from KBr(aq).** To a sample of each solution add dilute nitric acid (to remove carbonate and other interfering ions), then a few drops of aqueous silver nitrate, $\mathrm{AgNO_3(aq)}$:

- **KCl:** a **white precipitate** of silver chloride, $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgCl(s)}$. It **dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia** giving the colourless complex $[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2}]^+$.
- **KBr:** a **cream (pale yellow) precipitate** of silver bromide, $\mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + \mathrm{Br^-(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgBr(s)}$. It is **insoluble in dilute ammonia** (it dissolves only in concentrated ammonia).

Alternative test: add chlorine water, then a little hexane (or tetrachloromethane) and shake. KBr gives an orange-brown colour (bromine, orange-red in the organic layer), $\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{Br^-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^-} + \mathrm{Br_2}$; KCl shows no change.
